title: Five Camera Settings for Sharper Youth Sports Photos
body:
Most blurry sports photos are not the camera's fault. They come from a slow shutter speed, the wrong focus mode, or fear of high ISO. These five settings fix most of the problems I see from parents in the stands.

## 1. Use a fast shutter speed

Shutter speed controls motion blur, so it is the first setting to lock in. Canon pro photographer Jeff Swinger recommends a minimum of 1/1000 of a second to freeze game action [1]. Shotkit's sports guide agrees that 1/1000 is the standard and treats 1/500 as the lowest speed that still gives good results [2]. If you are new to manual settings, use shutter priority mode (Tv on Canon, S on Sony and Nikon) and set it to 1/1000.

## 2. Open the aperture all the way

A fast shutter lets in less light, so you need to make up for it. Set your aperture to the smallest f-number your lens allows, such as f/2.8 or f/4. Swinger notes that on kit zoom lenses, the widest aperture available at the long end of the zoom is the one to use [1]. A wide aperture also blurs the background, which helps your athlete stand out from the crowd.

## 3. Let the ISO climb

ISO is the setting most parents are afraid of, because higher numbers add grain. At a game, though, a little grain is better than a blurry photo. Swinger's advice is to set the shutter speed and aperture first and then raise the ISO until the exposure looks right, and he encourages photographers not to be afraid of high ISOs [1]. Auto ISO is a good option here, because the camera adjusts it for you as the light changes.

## 4. Switch to continuous autofocus

Single-shot autofocus locks onto one distance, so it falls behind as soon as a player moves. Continuous autofocus keeps adjusting while you hold the shutter button halfway down. Sony calls it AF-C, and Canon calls it AI Servo. Sony's autofocus guide for ball games recommends AF-C with tracking and human subject recognition turned on, so the focus point follows a player's face and eyes as they run [3].

## 5. Shoot in bursts and pick your spot

Set your camera to continuous drive mode and take short bursts of three to five frames during big moments. One of them will usually catch the peak of the action. Where you stand matters just as much. For night games, Swinger suggests shooting from the brighter side of the field and avoiding dark end zones, since many smaller stadiums do not light them well [1].

## Quick checklist

- Shutter speed: 1/1000 or faster
- Aperture: lowest f-number on your lens
- ISO: Auto, or as high as needed
- Focus: continuous (AF-C or AI Servo) with tracking
- Drive: continuous bursts

These settings will not replace a long telephoto lens, but they will make the photos you already take noticeably sharper. If you would rather watch the game and let someone else handle the camera, [send me your game details](#book).

## Sources

1. Swinger, Jeff. "Game Night: High Impact and High ISO Sports Photography." Canon U.S.A., 29 Aug. 2018. [usa.canon.com](https://www.usa.canon.com/learning/training-articles/training-articles-list/game-night-high-impact-and-high-iso-sports-photography)
2. Darrow, Ashley. "Best Shutter Speed for Sports Photography + Settings & Tips." Shotkit. [shotkit.com](https://shotkit.com/shutter-speed-sports/)
3. Sony Corporation. "Ball Games." Autofocus Settings Guide for Sports. [support.d-imaging.sony.co.jp](https://support.d-imaging.sony.co.jp/support/ilc/autofocus/ilce9m3/en/03.php)
